title: AS Paper 1 mock — Set A: Markets, consumer behaviour and the snack levy
description: A full 80-mark AS Paper 1 (Theme 1: Introduction to markets and market failure) to be sat in 90 minutes. Section A has four multiple-choice and four short-answer questions spanning the nature of economics, how markets work and market failure (aim for about 20-25 minutes). Section B is a data response on a fictional country's levy on high-sugar snacks covering elasticity, tax incidence, externalities, behavioural economics, government failure and alternative policies (about 65 minutes, after reading the extracts carefully). Show all calculations, draw and label diagrams fully, and make sure every 8+ mark answer uses the data and ends with a justified judgement.

questions.prompt: Economic theory predicts that, ceteris paribus, an increase in bus fares will reduce the number of bus journeys made. In one year a town's bus fares rose by 5%, yet the number of bus journeys increased. Which of the following is the most likely explanation that is consistent with the theory?
options: A Demand for bus travel in the town is price inelastic.
B The prediction is a normative statement, so it cannot be tested against evidence.
C Petrol prices and town-centre parking charges rose sharply in the same year.
D Bus operators earned more total revenue after the fare rise.
questions.explanation: The theory holds other things constant (ceteris paribus). If petrol prices and parking charges rose at the same time, the demand curve for bus travel (a substitute for driving) shifted to the right, which can outweigh the contraction caused by the fare rise. A is wrong: inelastic demand still means journeys fall, just proportionately less than price. B is wrong: the prediction is positive and testable. D describes a consequence of inelastic demand, not a reason journeys rose.

questions.prompt: An economy is currently producing at a point inside its production possibility frontier (PPF). Which of the following would move the economy towards its existing frontier without shifting the frontier?
options: A A fall in cyclical unemployment
B Net inward migration of working-age people
C The discovery of new reserves of natural gas
D An improvement in the quality of education and training
questions.explanation: A point inside the PPF shows unemployed or inefficiently used resources. Putting cyclically unemployed workers back to work uses existing resources more fully, moving the economy towards the frontier. B, C and D all increase the quantity or quality of the economy's resources, so they shift the PPF outwards.

questions.prompt: The demand curve for tickets to a music festival is a straight line. At a price of £60 no tickets would be demanded. At a price of £20, 4,000 tickets are sold. The organiser raises the price to £30 and sells 3,000 tickets. By how much does consumer surplus fall?
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the triangle between the demand curve and the price. At £20: 0.5 x 4,000 x (60 - 20) = £80,000. At £30: 0.5 x 3,000 x (60 - 30) = £45,000. The fall is £80,000 - £45,000 = £35,000. C is the new consumer surplus and D the original one; A is just the price rise x tickets lost.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best example of a public good?
options: A A flood defence wall that protects every property in a coastal town
B A seat on a crowded commuter train
C Treatment in a state-funded hospital
D A journey across a toll bridge
questions.explanation: A public good is non-rival (one person's benefit does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting). Once the flood wall is built, every property behind it is protected and no resident can be excluded, so there is a free-rider problem. A train seat is rival, hospital treatment is rival and could be charged for (it is state-provided, not a public good), and a toll bridge is excludable.

questions.prompt: Oakbridge Furniture, a manufacturer of kitchen units, has reorganised its factory so that each worker now performs a single repeated task, such as cutting, sanding or fitting hinges, instead of building a complete unit. Explain two possible disadvantages to the firm of this increased division of labour.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Division of labour means breaking production into separate tasks, with each worker specialising in one task (as described by Adam Smith in his pin factory example).
Application/Analysis (any two, developed in the context of Oakbridge): Repetitive, monotonous tasks may reduce motivation, raising absenteeism, staff turnover and recruitment costs, or causing more errors so the quality of units falls. Interdependence: production is a chain, so if one stage stops (for example the sanders are absent or a cutting machine breaks down) the whole line halts and output is lost. Loss of flexibility: workers who can only fit hinges cannot cover for absent colleagues or adapt quickly when the firm changes its product range. Workers lose broader craft skills, which may reduce job satisfaction and the firm's ability to offer bespoke units.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation. Advantages of division of labour gain no credit.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for an accurate definition of division of labour; 1 mark for identifying each of two relevant disadvantages (max 2); 1 mark for developing either disadvantage with a linked consequence for Oakbridge's costs, output or quality.

questions.prompt:
Priya is deciding how many fitness classes to attend each week. Each class costs £5. The table shows the total utility she gains, measured as the maximum amount of money (£) she would be willing to pay.

Classes per week | Total utility (£)
1 | 12
2 | 20
3 | 25
4 | 28

Using the table, explain how many classes per week Priya will attend if she is a rational consumer who aims to maximise her utility.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A rational consumer aims to maximise utility (net benefit) from limited income, so will consume an extra unit only if its marginal utility is at least equal to its price (the marginal cost to the consumer). Marginal utility diminishes as more is consumed.
Application: Marginal utility of each class = £12, £8, £5, £3.
Analysis: The first three classes each give marginal utility at least equal to the £5 price, so they add to (or do not reduce) her net benefit; total net benefit at 3 classes = £25 - £15 = £10. The fourth class gives only £3 of extra utility but costs £5, so attending it would reduce her net benefit by £2 (to £8). She therefore attends 3 classes. Accept 2 classes only if the student explains that she is exactly indifferent about the third class (marginal utility = price).
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge of utility maximisation (comparing marginal utility with price); 1 mark for correctly calculating marginal utilities; 1 mark for identifying 3 classes; 1 mark for explaining why the fourth class is not attended (marginal utility of £3 is below the £5 price, or reference to diminishing marginal utility).

questions.prompt: During a long summer heatwave, demand for electric fans in the UK increases sharply. Explain how the price mechanism may help to allocate resources in the market for electric fans.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The price mechanism is the way changes in prices, determined by the interaction of demand and supply, allocate scarce resources. It has three functions: signalling, incentive and rationing.
Application/Analysis (explained in the context of fans): Signalling: the rise in demand causes excess demand at the original price, so retailers raise prices; the higher price signals to producers and retailers that fans are scarce and highly valued. Incentive: higher prices raise expected profit, giving manufacturers and importers an incentive to increase output and shift stock into the UK (an extension of supply along the supply curve), drawing resources into fan production. Rationing: the higher price contracts demand, so the limited stock goes to consumers most willing and able to pay, eliminating the shortage at the new equilibrium. A diagram showing demand shifting right and price rising from P1 to P2 may be credited.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (definition of the price mechanism or identification of its functions); up to 3 marks for explaining the functions in the context of electric fans (1 mark per function clearly explained and applied, max 3).

questions.prompt: Explain how asymmetric information may lead to market failure in the market for household roof repairs.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Asymmetric information exists when one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other. Market failure occurs when the free market leads to a misallocation of resources (not allocatively efficient).
Application: The roofer can inspect the roof and knows what work is really needed and how well it has been done; most homeowners cannot safely check the roof or judge the quality of materials and workmanship.
Analysis: The roofer has an incentive to recommend unnecessary work or overcharge, so households over-consume repairs or pay more than the service is worth, and resources are wasted. Alternatively, homeowners who fear being cheated delay or avoid repairs that are genuinely needed, so too few repairs are bought, minor problems become costly damage and there is under-consumption. Either way the quantity traded differs from the socially optimal level, causing a welfare loss.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (definition of asymmetric information or market failure); 1 mark for application to roof repairs (who holds the better information); up to 2 marks for analysis (a developed chain explaining how the information gap leads to over- or under-consumption and a misallocation of resources).

questions.context:
Elsmere's levy on high-sugar snacks (illustrative data)

Table 1: The market for high-sugar snacks in Elsmere, before and after the levy (illustrative data)
Indicator | 2024 (before levy) | 2025 (after levy)
Average retail price per 100g pack (pence) | 80 | 96
Packs sold (millions per year) | 500 | 460
Levy per 100g pack (pence) | 0 | 20

Table 2: Diet-related health indicators in Elsmere (illustrative data)
Year | Adults classed as obese (%) | Children's hospital tooth extractions (thousands) | Estimated annual cost of diet-related illness to the Elsmere Health Service (£ billion)
2010 | 22 | 28 | 4.1
2015 | 24 | 32 | 4.9
2020 | 26 | 35 | 5.8
2024 | 27 | 37 | 6.6

Extract A: Why the government acted
Elsmere is a fictional country with a population of around 12 million and a tax-funded health service that is free at the point of use. In January 2025 its government introduced a levy of 20p on every 100g of confectionery, crisps and sweet biscuits containing more than 15g of sugar per 100g. The levy is paid by manufacturers and importers. Ministers argued that the costs of diet-related illness fall not only on the individuals concerned but on all taxpayers who fund the health service, and on employers who lose output when staff are ill. A government survey found that only around a third of adults could correctly interpret the sugar information on a snack wrapper, and most underestimated the calories in a typical pack. Snacks are often displayed at supermarket checkouts and sold in multi-buy deals, and around 40% of purchases are unplanned 'impulse' buys. Health researchers also point to the role of habit, and to a tendency for people to put far more weight on immediate enjoyment than on their long-term health. Revenue from the levy is earmarked for school sports facilities and free fruit in primary schools.

Extract B: Early concerns
After the levy's first year, critics say it is not working as intended. Households in the poorest fifth of the population spend around 4.5% of their food budget on high-sugar snacks, compared with around 2% for the richest fifth. Sales of untaxed sugary products such as cakes and pastries rose by around 6% in 2025, and some shoppers living near the border now buy snacks in a neighbouring country where there is no levy. Several manufacturers have cut pack sizes rather than raise prices further, and small independent retailers complain about the time spent working out which products are liable. Manufacturers say that reformulating recipes to fall below the 15g sugar threshold will take two to three years. Some health campaigners argue that the government should replace the levy with three alternative measures: a ban on displaying high-sugar snacks at checkouts and on multi-buy offers; compulsory 'traffic-light' labels on the front of every pack; and a subsidy to cut the price of fresh fruit and vegetables for low-income families.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: PED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price. Demand is price inelastic when the absolute value is less than 1.
Application: % change in quantity = (460 - 500) / 500 x 100 = -8%. % change in price = (96 - 80) / 80 x 100 = +20%. PED = -8 / 20 = -0.4 (price inelastic).
Analysis: A 20% rise in price cut consumption by only 8% (40 million fewer packs), so the levy changes behaviour relatively little; most of its effect is higher spending by consumers and revenue for the government rather than a large fall in consumption. Inelastic demand is consistent with habit and the lack of close substitutes for many consumers (Extract A). Credit recognition that the figure assumes ceteris paribus: other changes in 2025, such as shrinking pack sizes or substitution to untaxed cakes (Extract B), may distort the estimate.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for the PED formula; 1 mark for both percentage changes; 1 mark for PED = -0.4 (accept 0.4 if described as inelastic); up to 2 marks for explaining what inelastic demand implies for the levy's effect on consumption (1 for interpretation, 1 for a developed, contextual point).

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The incidence of a tax is the way its burden is shared between consumers and producers. A specific (per-unit) tax shifts supply vertically upwards by the amount of the tax.
Application: Total revenue = 20p x 460 million = £92 million. Price rose by 16p of the 20p levy, so consumers pay 16p x 460 million = £73.6 million (80%); producers bear 4p x 460 million = £18.4 million (20%).
Analysis: Demand is price inelastic (PED -0.4), so manufacturers can pass most of the levy on in higher prices without losing many sales; consumers have few close substitutes or buy out of habit. The more inelastic demand is relative to supply, the greater the share of the tax borne by consumers. A diagram with a steep demand curve and supply shifting up by 20p, showing the consumer and producer areas, may be credited.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge of tax incidence; 1 mark for total revenue of £92 million; 1 mark for consumer burden of £73.6 million (or 80%); up to 2 marks for explaining why consumers bear most of the levy (1 for linking to inelastic demand, 1 for development using PED -0.4 or the relative elasticities of demand and supply).

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Negative consumption externality: consumption imposes external costs on third parties, so marginal social benefit (MSB) is below marginal private benefit (MPB). Private versus external versus social costs and benefits. The free market produces where MPB = MPC; the social optimum is where MSB = MSC. Information failure and demerit goods.
Application: Health service is tax-funded and free at the point of use, so taxpayers bear treatment costs; employers lose output when staff are ill; the cost of diet-related illness rose from £4.1 billion in 2010 to £6.6 billion in 2024 (an increase of around 61%); adult obesity up from 22% to 27%; only a third of adults can interpret sugar labels.
Analysis: Diagram: MPB above MSB, MPC = MSC; free-market output Q1 where MPB = MPC exceeds the socially optimal Q* where MSB = MSC; welfare loss triangle between MSB and MSC from Q* to Q1 pointing towards the optimum. Chain: consumers weigh only their private enjoyment and price, ignoring the cost of their treatment to taxpayers and lost output for employers, so they buy beyond the point where the social benefit of the last pack equals its cost. Information failure strengthens this: consumers underestimate the private health cost, so perceived MPB exceeds true private benefit, adding further over-consumption.
Evaluation: Much of the cost of poor health (shorter life, lower earnings) falls on the consumer and is a private cost, not an externality, so the external element may be smaller than the £6.6 billion suggests. The health data show correlation, not causation: obesity and tooth decay also reflect inactivity and other foods and drinks, so not all costs can be attributed to snacks. External costs are hard to value in money terms, making the size of the welfare loss uncertain. Over-consumption may be better explained by behavioural factors than by an externality. Judgement on how significant the market failure is.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 5 marks; Evaluation up to 3 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (5 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Draws an accurate, fully labelled negative consumption externality diagram and explains it step by step, uses Table 2 (for example the 61% rise in costs) and Extract A to show who bears the external costs, separates private from external costs, and evaluates by questioning causation and the size of the external cost before judging that over-consumption is likely but its scale is uncertain.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Traditional theory assumes rational consumers who maximise utility with full information. Behavioural economics: bounded rationality, bounded self-control, biases (rules of thumb, anchoring, availability), the importance of habitual behaviour, social norms, framing, default choices and choice architecture.
Application: Only around a third of adults can interpret sugar labels and most underestimate calories; snacks displayed at checkouts; multi-buy deals; around 40% of purchases are impulse buys; habit; greater weight on immediate enjoyment than long-term health; PED of -0.4 (Table 1) suggests purchases are not very responsive to price.
Analysis: Bounded rationality: consumers lack the time or ability to process nutritional information, so they rely on rules of thumb and misjudge the true cost to their health. Bounded self-control and present bias: the pleasure is immediate while health costs are distant, so consumers buy more than they would plan to when thinking calmly, and later regret it. Habit: repeated purchases become automatic, reducing responsiveness to price (helping explain inelastic demand). Choice architecture: placement at checkouts when shoppers are tired triggers impulse buying; multi-buy deals frame extra packs as a saving and anchor on the 'normal' price. Social norms: snacking may be the accepted behaviour at work or among friends. Each leads to consumption beyond the level that maximises the consumer's own long-term utility, a source of market failure separate from externalities.
Evaluation: Some consumption reflects an informed, rational choice to enjoy snacks now, so not all purchases are against consumers' interests; judging what is 'in their interest' involves a value judgement. The relative importance of each bias may differ between groups, for example children and adults, or low- and high-income households. Evidence is partly from surveys and may not show actual behaviour. Behavioural explanations suggest nudges such as moving snacks away from checkouts may be cheap and effective, but habits are hard to change, as the small 8% fall in sales after a 20% price rise suggests. Justified view on which factor matters most.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Contrasts the rational-consumer model with at least two or three clearly defined behavioural concepts, each linked to specific evidence in Extract A (the 40% impulse purchases, the third of adults who can read labels), explains through full chains why each causes over-consumption against the consumer's own interest, and evaluates by weighing the relative importance of the biases and questioning whether all consumption is irrational.

Several manufacturers have cut pack sizes rather than raise prices further, and small independent retailers complain about the time spent working out which products are liable. Manufacturers say that reformulating recipes to fall below the 15g sugar threshold will take two to three years. Some health campaigners argue that the government should replace the levy with three alternative measures: a ban on displaying high-sugar snacks at checkouts and on multi-buy offers; compulsory 'traffic-light' labels on the front of every pack; and a subsidy to cut the price of fresh fruit and vegetables for low-income families.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Government failure: intervention that leads to a net welfare loss, or a less efficient allocation of resources than the free market would have produced. Causes: distortion of price signals, unintended consequences, excessive administrative costs, information gaps.
Application: Untaxed cakes and pastries up around 6%; cross-border shopping; manufacturers cutting pack sizes; administrative burden on small retailers; poorest fifth spend 4.5% of food budget on snacks versus 2% for the richest; reformulation will take two to three years; 15g threshold; consumption fell only 8% (Table 1).
Analysis: Unintended consequences: substitution towards untaxed sugary foods means total sugar intake may barely fall, so external costs persist while consumers pay more; cross-border shopping shifts spending abroad, reducing Elsmere retailers' revenue without cutting consumption. Information gaps: the government cannot measure the marginal external cost accurately, so a 20p levy may be too low or too high; the 15g threshold is arbitrary, so products just below it escape. Equity: the levy is regressive, taking a larger share of income from poorer households. Administrative and compliance costs for small retailers reduce the net benefit. Shrinking pack sizes may reduce sugar per pack, which could be a positive unintended consequence.
Evaluation: Government failure requires a net welfare loss, which is not shown: consumption has fallen by 40 million packs and £92 million is raised and earmarked for school sports and fruit, which may reduce future health costs. It is early: reformulation within two to three years may cut sugar content substantially, so long-run effects may be larger than first-year data suggest. Regressivity may be offset because poorer households, with higher obesity risk, gain most of the health benefits, and the revenue use is progressive. Some problems (substitution, threshold) could be fixed by widening the levy's base rather than abolishing it. Judgement: some elements of government failure, but probably partial rather than a net welfare loss.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Defines government failure precisely as a net welfare loss, analyses at least two distinct types (unintended consequences, information gaps, administrative costs) each supported with figures from Extract B and Table 1, and evaluates by weighing these against the gains (fall in sales, revenue use, future reformulation) to conclude whether the levy is a partial failure that can be corrected by redesign.

Extract A: Why the government acted
Elsmere is a fictional country with a population of around 12 million and a tax-funded health service that is free at the point of use. In January 2025 its government introduced a levy of 20p on every 100g of confectionery, crisps and sweet biscuits containing more than 15g of sugar per 100g. The levy is paid by manufacturers and importers. Ministers argued that the costs of diet-related illness fall not only on the individuals concerned but on all taxpayers who fund the health service, and on employers who lose output when staff are ill. A government survey found that only around a third of adults could correctly interpret the sugar information on a snack wrapper, and most underestimated the calories in a typical pack. Snacks are often displayed at supermarket checkouts and sold in multi-buy deals, and around 40% of purchases are unplanned 'impulse' buys. Health researchers also point to the role of habit, and to a tendency for people to put far more weight on immediate enjoyment than on their long-term health. Revenue from the levy is earmarked for school sports facilities and free fruit in primary schools.

Extract B: Early concerns
After the levy's first year, critics say it is not working as intended. Households in the poorest fifth of the population spend around 4.5% of their food budget on high-sugar snacks, compared with around 2% for the richest fifth. Sales of untaxed sugary products such as cakes and pastries rose by around 6% in 2025, and some shoppers living near the border now buy snacks in a neighbouring country where there is no levy. Several manufacturers have cut pack sizes rather than raise prices further, and small independent retailers complain about the time spent working out which products are liable. Manufacturers say that reformulating recipes to fall below the 15g sugar threshold will take two to three years. Some health campaigners argue that the government should replace the levy with three alternative measures: a ban on displaying high-sugar snacks at checkouts and on multi-buy offers; compulsory 'traffic-light' labels on the front of every pack; and a subsidy to cut the price of fresh fruit and vegetables for low-income families.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Indirect taxes to internalise external costs; regulation (restrictions on display and promotions); provision of information (labelling); subsidies; how each corrects market failure caused by externalities, information gaps and behavioural biases. Diagrams: tax shifting supply up by the levy; information shifting perceived MPB left towards MSB; subsidy shifting supply of fruit and vegetables right.
Application: Levy of 20p per 100g pack; PED of -0.4 and an 8% fall in sales; revenue of £92 million earmarked for school sports and fruit; 80% of the levy passed on to consumers; regressive pattern (4.5% versus 2% of food budgets); substitution to cakes (+6%) and cross-border shopping; 40% impulse buys; only a third of adults understand labels; health costs of £6.6 billion.
Analysis: Levy: raises price, reducing quantity towards the social optimum; provides a continuous incentive to reformulate; raises revenue that can be spent on health-promoting programmes; but with inelastic demand the fall in consumption is small. Checkout and multi-buy ban: targets impulse purchases (40%) and present bias directly, at little cost to the government; does not raise prices, so it is less regressive. Traffic-light labels: reduce the information gap, shifting demand (perceived MPB) towards MSB; low cost to the state but costs for firms. Fruit and vegetable subsidy: reduces the price of healthier substitutes, encouraging switching and improving diets of low-income families; diagram showing supply shifting right and the subsidy cost to government; but requires funding, which the levy currently provides.
Evaluation: Effectiveness depends on the cause of over-consumption: if mainly behavioural and informational, regulation and labelling address the root causes better than price; if externalities dominate, a tax is the most direct way to internalise them. Measures could be combined rather than treated as alternatives: levy revenue (£92 million) could fund the subsidy. Time: labelling and display bans act quickly; reformulation triggered by the levy takes two to three years. Enforcement and administrative costs differ; display bans are easy to monitor in large stores but hard in small shops. Risk of government failure: regulation can also have unintended consequences (promotions move online). Equity: removing the levy removes a regressive tax but also its revenue. Prioritised, justified conclusion, for example keep the levy but widen its base and add display bans and labels, with revenue funding the subsidy.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 12 marks; Evaluation up to 8 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-3 marks): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no application to the context; analysis is descriptive or confused.
KAA Level 2 (4-6 marks): Mostly accurate knowledge with some application to the context and data; chains of reasoning are partial or not clearly linked to the question; diagrams, if used, contain errors or are not explained.
KAA Level 3 (7-9 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with relevant use of data from the extracts; several developed chains of reasoning, though some lack depth or balance; diagrams are mostly accurate and referred to.
KAA Level 4 (10-12 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout, integrating data from the extracts; fully developed, coherent chains of reasoning covering both sides of the issue; accurate diagrams are integrated into the argument.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluative comments are generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; no supported judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation addresses relevant issues with some support from the extracts, but is not fully developed, not prioritised or lacks a clear final judgement.
Evaluation Level 3 (7-8 marks): Sustained, well-supported evaluation that weighs the arguments, prioritises the most significant factors, recognises what the answer depends on and reaches a fully justified judgement.
A* answer: Analyses the levy and each of the three alternatives with accurate diagrams, ties each policy to a specific cause of the market failure using data (PED -0.4, 40% impulse buys, 4.5% versus 2% spending shares, £92 million revenue), evaluates throughout using magnitude, time lags, cost, equity and the risk of government failure, and reaches a clear, prioritised judgement, typically that a combined package is superior to choosing one or the other.
